text: Johnson O'Connor (January 22, 1891 – July 1, 1973) was an American psychometrician, researcher, and educator best known as a pioneer in aptitude testing and a strong advocate for the importance of vocabulary. Born into a prosperous Chicago family, he was the son of John O’Connor and Nelie Johnson O’Connor; his mother descended from early Puritan settlers of Massachusetts, and his father was an attorney who once shared an office with Clarence Darrow. O’Connor received a progressive education at the University of Chicago Laboratory School under John Dewey and graduated from Harvard University in 1913 with a degree in Philosophy. He later conducted research in astronomical mathematics under Percival Lowell and worked in electrical engineering at American Steel and Wire and General Electric. In 1922, F.P. Cox of General Electric commissioned O’Connor to develop the "human" engineering project, which aimed to match employees to positions aligned with their natural abilities and retrain them in those areas. This led O’Connor to study inborn aptitudes and create aptitude tests known as "work samples," developing classifications such as "Graphoria," "Ideaphoria," and "Structural Visualization." He became one of the first researchers to provide evidence that aptitudes are innate, showing that individuals with higher mathematical aptitude learn mathematics more efficiently than those with lower aptitude, and that despite equal training, those with higher aptitude consistently outperform others. In 1930, O’Connor founded the Human Engineering Laboratory at Stevens Institute of Technology, which later became the Johnson O'Connor Research Foundation, a non-profit with aptitude testing centers in major U.S. cities. While studying aptitudes related to specific vocations, he discovered that vocabulary level was the strongest single predictor of occupational success across all fields, and that vocabulary is not innate but can be acquired by anyone. This finding became central to his later work, where he focused on cataloging essential English words and ordering them by difficulty. He developed a method to assess students’ vocabulary levels through a multiple-choice diagnostic test, recommending that students enter a vocabulary program at a level matching their skill, with optimal learning occurring just beyond that level. He authored several books on vocabulary, including "The Johnson O'Connor English Vocabulary Builder," "The Johnson O'Connor Science Vocabulary Builder," and the "Ginn Vocabulary Building Program" (co-authored). His extensive vocabulary was notably showcased during a guest appearance on Groucho Marx’s "You Bet Your Life," where Groucho humorously remarked on his dual last names. In his final years, O’Connor continued researching, lecturing, and writing on human aptitudes and mental potential, publishing books such as "Structural Visualization," "The Unique Individual," and "Psychometrics." He also focused on vocabulary acquisition processes. O’Connor died in Mexico City, D.F., on July 1, 1973, and is buried beside his wife, architect Eleanor Manning O’Connor, in Newport Beach, California. He was survived by his son, Chadwell O’Connor, an engineer and Academy Award winner who designed the O'Connor Fluid-Head camera tripod.
